analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal standards requiring cars to meet fuel efficiency targets.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee but never received a vote, so fuel economy standards remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out the corporate average fuel economy standards, the federal rules that require carmakers' fleets to average a minimum number of miles per gallon. Those standards push automakers to sell more efficient vehicles, which lowers gasoline bills for drivers. The bill was sent to committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Automakers, which would no longer face penalties for selling fleets that average fewer miles per gallon, and oil producers, which would see somewhat higher gasoline demand. Drivers would pay more at the pump over time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have repealed federal requirements that automakers' fleets meet average miles-per-gallon targets, freeing manufacturers from those compliance obligations.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, through higher lifetime gasoline costs, and the public through increased fuel consumption and emissions.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the standards would allow new cars to travel fewer miles per gallon, raising gasoline costs for drivers over the life of each vehicle.
It would remove a main federal tool for reducing oil consumption and vehicle emissions, with costs borne by consumers and the public in fuel spending and pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is little to weigh: the bill would have saved carmakers compliance costs at the price of higher fuel bills for drivers and more pollution, and in any case it never advanced beyond a committee referral, so it had no practical effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and its subcommittee, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on February 8, 2022, with one Republican cosponsor.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the next day to its Consumer Protection and Commerce Subcommittee.
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fuel economy standards stayed in force, so consumers keep the fuel savings the standards require; automakers remain subject to compliance costs.

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the corporate average fuel economy standards.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed carmakers from fuel economy compliance requirements, letting them sell less efficient vehicles without penalties. Because the bill never advanced, current standards remain.
Weaker fuel economy standards mean more gasoline demand over time. The bill died, so nothing changed.
